files.name: AdminController.cs

notes.8: The action handler — note there is no authorization attribute on it or the controller.
notes.10: Deletes the user with the given id.

options.label: A very large `id` could overflow the int
options.whyWrong: Integer range isn't the issue; the lack of an access check is.

options.label: The action deletes any user but carries no authentication or authorization check, so any caller — not just admins — can invoke it
Returning `Ok()` reveals that the user existed
options.whyWrong: An information nuance is trivial next to anyone being able to delete accounts.

options.label: Rename the route to something non-guessable
options.whyWrong: Security by obscurity; once the route is discovered it's still wide open.

options.label: Require an admin role on the controller/action
Validate that id is positive
options.whyWrong: Input validation doesn't control who is allowed to delete users.

options.label: Return 404 instead of 200 after deleting
options.whyWrong: Changing the response status adds no access check.

training.exploit: Send `POST /api/admin/users/1/delete` with no token or a non-admin token. With no `[Authorize]` on the controller or action, ASP.NET runs it for anyone who can reach the URL, deleting arbitrary accounts (a function-level access-control failure).

hints.line: What's missing above the privileged action?
hints.bugClass: A sensitive action with no permission gate.
hints.why: Who is allowed to call this endpoint as written?
hints.fix: Require the appropriate role to reach it.

writeup.summary: `DeleteUser` performs a privileged operation but neither the controller nor the action has any `[Authorize]` attribute, so it runs for any caller — a missing function-level authorization check. The fix applies `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` (ideally at the controller) so only administrators can invoke it. Obscure routes, id validation, and response-code changes do not restrict who may act.
